title: Remittances and the cost of sending money home
bodyMd:
Every year migrant workers send home sums that dwarf the official aid budgets of the countries they left. Transfers of this kind, known as remittances, are estimated to have reached 670 billion dollars worldwide last year, of which roughly four fifths flowed to low- and middle-income economies. In a handful of small states they amount to more than a quarter of national income.

What makes remittances unusual is how they behave in a downturn. Foreign direct investment tends to retreat when a recipient economy weakens; remittances often rise, because migrants send more precisely when their families need it most. Economists call this counter-cyclicality, and it is the main reason development agencies treat remittances as a stabilising flow rather than a speculative one.

The friction is cost. The global average charge for sending 200 dollars still sits at about 6.2 per cent, more than double the 3 per cent target that governments set for themselves under the Sustainable Development Goals. That average hides wide variation. Corridors served by many competing operators, such as the one running from the Gulf states to South Asia, cost under 4 per cent; several intra-African corridors exceed 8 per cent. Mobile money has narrowed the gap where it has been allowed to compete, but in some markets banks hold exclusive agreements with payment networks, and where that exclusivity holds, prices have barely moved in a decade.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about remittances, the money migrant workers send to their home countries. There is no figure, table or mathematical notation. The passage gives four numerical facts in words: worldwide remittances of about 670 billion dollars last year, of which about four fifths went to low- and middle-income economies; more than a quarter of national income in a few small states; a global average transfer charge of about 6.2 per cent on a 200 dollar transfer against a 3 per cent international target; and a range of corridor charges from under 4 per cent between the Gulf states and South Asia to over 8 per cent within parts of Africa.
